question_en:
I am helping a maritime museum verify a display panel for an old wooden boat. The attachments show its current open hull, the short number on the bow, and its historical appearance after modification. Please answer the following questions:

1. Please confirm the boat's original name, official service number, builder, year built, boat type, original lifeboat station, and years in service.
2. When was the boat retired, and when was it moved to the current museum? Please explain which structures from its service period are now missing, what was added after retirement, and which parts were later removed during conservation and restoration.

Answer format: Please answer using numbered points (1)–(2). Each point should only answer the corresponding sub-question and provide all information required by that question.
answer:
(1) Original name: CHARTERHOUSE; Official service number: RNLI Official Number 563; Builder: Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company, Blackwall; Year built: 1908; Boat type: 40-foot self-righting lifeboat; Original lifeboat station: Fishguard, Pembrokeshire; Years in service: 1909–1930.

(2) Retirement: September 1930; Moved to current museum: Relocated to the West Wales Maritime Museum in Pembroke Dock in 2019, officially welcomed on February 14, 2020, with the formal donation completed in February 2023. Parts missing from the original service structure: deck beams, bulkheads, and other deck structures; only some deck planks and hatches survived. Additions after retirement: During conversion to a private yacht in 1931, an enclosed cabin and superstructure were added, and a diesel engine was installed. Removals during subsequent conservation and restoration: Starting in 2009, during the conservation phase by the Goodwick / Charterhouse Returns Trust, the added yacht superstructure was removed.

# Detailed Simulated Retrieval Trajectory · P2-8-2-F04

## Step 01 · Separately observe the current hull, the short stem number, and the historical appearance

Action: Examine the three current inputs: the open wooden hull, the short number on the stem, and the old photograph showing an enclosed cabin. First, record their differences, without treating the historical photograph as the current state.

Evidence observation: The open hull and the historical cabin show that more than one stage is involved. The short number TL1 on the bow can serve as a lead for finding shipbuilding records. Example query: early RNLI motor lifeboat builder number TL1.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/sites/default/files/2024-04/charterhouse5.jpg
https://imagecdn.websitebuilder.prositehosting.co.uk/4b/c2/4bc22e1c-53d0-40de-8c0d-ae152d55a93d.jpg
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/sites/default/files/2019-11/Converted%20to%20the%20yacht%20Marian%201960s.png

Result of this step: Candidates point to an early RNLI lifeboat and a later private yacht conversion.

## Step 02 · Use TL1 to search the museum's records for the same vessel

Action: Check the Charterhouse page of the West Wales Maritime Heritage Society, comparing the original image showing the hull treatment and the explanation of the stem number.

Evidence observation: The museum refers to TL1 as the builder's number carved on the stem. It is a builder's number and cannot directly answer the RNLI Official Number asked in the question. The page name Charterhouse provides the vessel name for the next step.

Evidence links:
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse
https://imagecdn.websitebuilder.prositehosting.co.uk/4b/c2/4bc22e1c-53d0-40de-8c0d-ae152d55a93d.jpg

Result of this step: Establish the relationship between TL1 and Charterhouse, then go to the official registration page to check the official service number.

## Step 03 · Open the National Historic Ships registration page to confirm identity

Action: Example query: National Historic Ships Charterhouse RNLI Official Number 563. Verify against the current status image of the same vessel, the original name, and the main registration text.

Evidence observation: The formal record shows the original name CHARTERHOUSE; the RNLI Official Number is 563. The 3611 in the National Historic Ships webpage path is the registration entry ID for that website, not the RNLI service number. The three numbers TL1, 563, and 3611 must not be mixed.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/sites/default/files/2024-04/charterhouse5.jpg
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse

Result of this step: The original name and official service number for sub-question 1 are confirmed.

## Step 04 · Extract builder, location, year, and boat type

Action: Read the complete shipyard name, Blackwall location, year 1908, and 40-foot boat type from the builder field and historical narrative on the registration page.

Evidence observation: Builder: Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company, Blackwall; Year built: 1908; Boat type: 40-foot self-righting lifeboat. Do not write 1909 (the start of service) as the year built, nor treat the later added yacht cabin as the original boat type.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse

Result of this step: All four builder attributes for sub-question 1 are complete.

## Step 05 · Trace the lifeboat period history to find the original station and service interval

Action: Read the narrative regarding the 1909 naming/commissioning and the Fishguard station, and verify the retirement node.

Evidence observation: Original lifeboat station: Fishguard, Pembrokeshire; Years in service: 1909–1930. Construction was completed in a different year from the start of service; these dates belong respectively in the fields for year built and years in service.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse

Result of this step: All fields for sub-question 1 can now be filled.

## Step 06 · Verify the specific month of retirement

Action: Search the original registration history for records of termination of RNLI service, distinguishing between retirement and sale for conversion.

Evidence observation: Retirement was in September 1930; the sale to a private owner and the start of yacht conversion in 1931 are subsequent events. The sale year must not be treated as the retirement year.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse

Result of this step: The retirement time for sub-question 2 is precise to the month and year.

## Step 07 · Verify the MARIAN phase using captions on historical photographs

Action: Open the photograph captioned "Converted to the yacht Marian 1960s" and compare the cabin and superstructure with the input historical photograph.

Evidence observation: This photograph shows the appearance after conversion to the private yacht MARIAN; the 1960s in the photo caption is the period when the photo was taken or the appearance recorded, not the year conversion started in 1931. The photo date must not override the text-recorded conversion node.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/sites/default/files/2019-11/Converted%20to%20the%20yacht%20Marian%201960s.png
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse

Result of this step: Confirm that the historical photograph belongs to the post-retirement yacht phase.

## Step 08 · Read conversion details and address year discrepancies in the name table

Action: Check the 1931 conversion described in the registration text and museum narrative, then compare with the name history table.

Evidence observation: After being sold in 1931, it was converted into a private motor yacht, adding an enclosed cabin, superstructure, and installing a diesel engine; the registration name table records Marian starting from 1932. For the current question regarding the year and content of the conversion, use 1931 from the main text; do not confuse the start year in the name table with the same event.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse

Result of this step: Added structures and original lifeboat structures are accounted for separately.

## Step 09 · Query the 2009 restoration of the original name and conservation phase

Action: Example query: Charterhouse Returns Trust Goodwick 2009 superstructure removed. Read the donation and conservation history.

Evidence observation: In 2009, it entered the Charterhouse Returns Trust/Goodwick conservation phase and the original name Charterhouse was restored; the preservation registration records that the added yacht superstructure was removed during this phase. Do not attribute all structures currently missing to removal by the current museum.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse

Result of this step: The removal of the added superstructure has a specific period and institutional context.

## Step 10 · Verify the year of relocation to the current museum

Action: Open the West Wales Maritime Heritage Society project page on National Historic Ships and read the 2019 relocation record.

Evidence observation: The project page states it was relocated to the West Wales Maritime Museum in Pembroke Dock in 2019. This describes the physical move node and should be distinguished from the formal welcome ceremony and property donation.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/shipshape/projects/west-wales-maritime-heritage-society-pembrokeshire-charterhouse

Result of this step: The main year for "when moved to the current museum" is 2019.

## Step 11 · Complete the 2020 welcome and 2023 donation nodes

Action: Return to the registration page and museum history to compare subsequent dates, avoiding combining three types of dates into a single contradictory answer.

Evidence observation: 2020-02-14 was the formal welcome; the formal donation was completed in February 2023. Together with the 2019 relocation, these constitute three distinct events; stating them separately explains why multiple dates for the current museum appear in the data.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/shipshape/projects/west-wales-maritime-heritage-society-pembrokeshire-charterhouse

Result of this step: The timeline is 2019 relocation → 2020 welcome → 2023 formal donation.

## Step 12 · Read the status of missing original deck structures

Action: Compare the current image of the open hull item-by-item with the registration page's narrative regarding original structures such as deck beams and bulkheads.

Evidence observation: Deck structures such as deck beams and bulkheads from the original service period are missing; only some deck planks and hatches survived. Public narratives describe the missing status, but one must not infer which specific component was removed by which conservation project solely because the photograph appears empty.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/sites/default/files/2024-04/charterhouse5.jpg

Result of this step: Missing original structures and removal of added structures are not conflated into a single item.

## Step 13 · Organize the three structural states into a verifiable comparison

Action: Review the data by categorizing into: originally present but now missing, added during private conversion, and removed during the conservation phase.

Evidence observation: Originally missing: deck beams, bulkheads, etc.; Added in 1931: enclosed cabin/superstructure and diesel engine; Subsequently removed: the added yacht superstructure. The current status in the image only assists comparison; specific event attribution is supported by registration and museum texts.

Evidence links:
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/sites/default/files/2024-04/charterhouse5.jpg
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/sites/default/files/2019-11/Converted%20to%20the%20yacht%20Marian%201960s.png

Result of this step: Structural changes for sub-question 2 are narrated in chronological order without over-attribution.

## Step 14 · Verify the preservation environment using the museum's on-site description

Action: View the open conservation shed and exhibition venue information on the visitus page, and understand the state of the open hull in combination with the current land-based conservation plan.

Evidence observation: The current museum provides the context for land-based preservation and display; the data emphasizes retaining original materials and making internal engineering structures visible; this does not mean the boat has been returned to service or restored to the complete appearance of the original lifeboat. The question also does not request a return-to-service plan.

Evidence links:
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/visitus
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse

Result of this step: The on-site environment serves only to preserve context; no unsupported restoration results are added.

## Step 15 · Distinguish evidence specific to the single boat from general RNLI historical data

Action: Examine the role of the RNLI history FAQ in the source ledger to avoid inferring this boat's unique identity from general materials.

Evidence observation: General RNLI history/drawing materials indicate the scope of archives available for future reference; they do not independently prove the identity of CHARTERHOUSE, nor do they make TL1 undisputed evidence of being the "first motor lifeboat in the UK." The current question does not ask about such rankings, so no additional conclusions should be drawn.

Evidence links:
https://rnli.org/about-us/our-history/faqs
https://www.nationalhistoricships.org.uk/register/3611/charterhouse
https://www.wwmhs.org.uk/boat-charterhouse

Result of this step: The final answer covers only this boat's identity and the time/structural changes required by the question.

## Step 16 · Verify question requirements and output scope

Action: Map each publicly required item to the evidence above one by one, checking the total count, positive/negative items, and field formats.

Evidence observation: Sub-question 1 has seven identity fields; sub-question 2 covers retirement, three dates related to the current museum, missing original structures, 1931 additions, and removals starting in 2009. The years 1930/1931/1932 and 2019/2020/2023 each carry independent event semantics.

Result of this step: Write only the requested information into the final answer; keep the search process and exclusion criteria in the trajectory.

## Step 17 · Final answer

(1) Original name: CHARTERHOUSE; Official service number: RNLI Official Number 563; Builder: Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company, Blackwall; Year built: 1908; Boat type: 40-foot self-righting lifeboat; Original lifeboat station: Fishguard, Pembrokeshire; Years in service: 1909–1930.

(2) Retirement: September 1930; Moved to current museum: Relocated to the West Wales Maritime Museum in Pembroke Dock in 2019, officially welcomed on February 14, 2020, with the formal donation completed in February 2023. Parts missing from the original service structure: deck beams, bulkheads, and other deck structures; only some deck planks and hatches survived. Additions after retirement: During conversion to a private yacht in 1931, an enclosed cabin and superstructure were added, and a diesel engine was installed. Removals during subsequent conservation and restoration: Starting in 2009, during the conservation phase by the Goodwick / Charterhouse Returns Trust, the added yacht superstructure was removed.
